citation: Krueger, A. B. (1999). Experimental estimates of education production functions. QJE.
subject: Math and Reading
ell_context: Low ELL share in TN in 1980s
attrition: Substantial attrition across grades K to 3
compliance_issue: Non-compliance with reassignments to small classes
primary_author_claim: Small classes (13-17) increase test scores by 0.20 SD in K-3
major_criticism: Hawthorne effects; teacher and student non-random switching
us_external_validity: Direct U.S. experimental evidence; compares 15 vs 22 (not 25 vs 30)

citation: Chetty, R., et al. (2011). How does your kindergarten classroom affect your life? Evidence from Project STAR. QJE.
subject: Adult Outcomes
attrition: Sample attrition tracked through tax records
primary_author_claim: Small kindergarten class assignment increases college enrollment and adult outcomes
replication_status: Replicated via IRS tax record link
major_criticism: Test score fadeout occurs by grade 8 despite long-term gain
notes: Demonstrates long-term non-cognitive benefits despite score fadeout

citation: Hoxby, C. M. (2000). The effects of class size on student achievement: New evidence from population variation. QJE.
subject: Reading and Math
identification_strategy: Idiosyncratic cohort population variation and class size rules
primary_author_claim: Class size reductions over the 15-30 range do not raise achievement
major_criticism: Potential measurement error in cohort smoothing
us_external_validity: Identifies variation in U.S. classrooms across the 15 to 30 student range
notes: Critical test of 15-30 student variation in U.S. context

citation: Angrist, J. D., & Lavy, V. (1999). Using Maimonides' rule to estimate the effect of class size on scholastic achievement. QJE.
subject: Math and Reading
primary_author_claim: Class size reduction at the 40-student rule cutoff significantly increases achievement
replication_status: Subject to re-estimation by Angrist et al. (2019)

us_external_validity: Israel structural differences from U.S. (40-student cap vs U.S. norms)

citation: Angrist, J. D., et al. (2019). Maimonides' Rule Redux. Journal of Econometrics.
subject: Math and Reading
identification_strategy: Replication and extension of Maimonides rule with donut RD
primary_author_claim: Earlier large effects attenuate substantially once enrollment sorting is addressed
major_criticism: Highlights sensitivity of RDD to enrollment manipulation near threshold
us_external_validity: Demonstrates fragility of RDD estimates when boundary sorting exists
notes: Shows importance of auditing original findings

citation: Blatchford, P., et al. (2003). Are class size differences related to pupils' educational progress and classroom processes? BERJ.
subject: Math and Literacy

compliance_issue: Smaller classes produce substantially more one-on-one teacher interaction and feedback
replication_status: Observational allocation of students across schools
major_criticism: Anglosphere primary system; illuminates mechanistic attention constraints
us_external_validity: Pioneering mechanistic evidence on teacher attention

citation: Chingos, M. M. (2012). The impact of a universal class-size reduction policy: Evidence from Florida's statewide mandate. Econ of Ed Review.

citation: Jepsen, C., & Rivkin, S. (2009). Class size reduction and student achievement: Teacher quality tradeoff. Econometrica.

citation: Urquiola, M. (2006). Identifying class size effects in developing countries: The presence of private schools. AER.

replication_status: Influential critique of Maimonides RD designs

us_external_validity: Methodological warning on parental sorting around capacity cutoffs

citation: Han, E., & Ryu, H. (2017). Effects of class size reduction in upper grades: Evidence from Seoul, Korea. Economics of Education Review.
subject: Reading Math and English
identification_strategy: 2002 Seoul CSR policy reducing 10th grade classes from 44 to 35 plus within-school random assignment
outcome: CSAT College Scholastic Ability Test Scores
primary_author_claim: Reducing high school class size from 44 to 35 yielded small effects (<0.02 SD per 10 students)
major_criticism: High baseline class size (44 to 35) and extensive private tutoring in Korea
us_external_validity: Upper secondary evidence; margin tested is 44 to 35 distinct from U.S. 25 to 35
notes: Critical upper-secondary high school causal benchmark directly measuring 10th-12th grade departmentalized instruction

citation: Denny, K., & Oppedisano, V. (2013). The duality of class size: The effect of class size on cognitive and non-cognitive skills. Labour Economics.
subject: Math and Science (PISA)
identification_strategy: Cross-cohort variation in enrollment instrumenting for 15-year-old class size in PISA
outcome: PISA Math and Science Test Scores
compliance_issue: Weak instrument issues in U.S. PISA sample
primary_author_claim: Secondary class size effects are modest and show trade-offs between cognitive and non-cognitive outcomes
major_criticism: U.S. IV estimates are statistically imprecise; school-level sampling in PISA
us_external_validity: Explicitly tests 15-year-olds in U.S. and U.K. departmentalized secondary schools
notes: One of the few causal IV studies on 15-year-olds (Grade 9/10) in the U.S.

citation: Akabayashi, H., & Nakamura, R. (2014). Can small class sizes reduce achievement gaps? Evidence from statutory class-size rules in Japan. Economics of Education Review.
subject: Math and Japanese
identification_strategy: Statutory maximum class size cap of 40 in Japanese lower secondary schools
primary_author_claim: Lower secondary class size reductions at the 40-student margin have small to null effects on achievement
major_criticism: High baseline cap (40 students); homogeneous curriculum
us_external_validity: Departmentalized lower secondary grades (7-9); cap is 40 rather than U.S. 25-35
notes: Narrows the secondary void for lower secondary grades 7-9; confirms small effects around cap of 40

citation: Cohen-Zada, D., Gradstein, M., & Reuven, E. (2013). Class size and the regression discontinuity design: The case of public schools. IZA DP No. 4679 / Oxford Bulletin.
